question: The war in Ukraine, the flare-up in the Middle East and the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz have triggered a continuing energy crisis with unbearable economic consequences for households and businesses. Electricity prices have skyrocketed. In this context, it is essential to create a permanent European mechanism to protect households and businesses, which will prevent extreme increases in electricity prices.

Such a mechanism would be activated when prices exceed pre-defined levels and would allow, on the basis of clear European rules, the immediate mobilisation of resources to support consumers and businesses. It cannot be that every new energy crisis finds Europe searching for emergency solutions from scratch. A permanent safety net is needed, which will be activated when there is a real need. Given this: 1.
Is the Commission considering the creation of a permanent European mechanism to protect consumers and businesses from future energy crises and extreme price increases?
Does the Commission intend to make additional European resources available to support households and businesses to address energy costs in periods of sharp price increases?
What measures does the Commission intend to take by 2027 to substantially reduce the cost of electricity bills for households and businesses?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.11.2026) Article 66a of Directive (EU) 2019/9441 provides for the possibility for the Council, on a proposal from the Commission, to declare an electricity price crisis where criteria2 are met. The Commission continues to monitor developments in energy prices and their implications for citizens.

In April 2026, the Commission presented the AccelerateEU communication3 which set out actions for implementation by Member States to protect families and businesses against energy price shocks and supply disruptions created by EU dependency on imported fossil fuel. In May 2026, it presented a catalogue4 of measures that can be replicated to protect consumers and save energy.

These should be funded by Member States or through existing EU programmes. In addition, the Commission adopted the Middle East Crisis Temporary State Aid Framework, allowing Member States to support sectors affected by rising energy costs as well as increased electricity-price relief for energy-intensive industries5.

It also has enabled6 Member States to request an extension of the scope of the National Escape Clause under EU fiscal rules to cover eligible energy-security measures aimed at strengthening energy-system resilience and reducing dependence on fossil fuels. In addition to the above, the Commission presented a proposal7 to future-proof electricity bills.

It aims to lower electricity costs through network charges that encourage flexible, system-friendly grid use and the efficient integration of generation and demand. The proposal includes a provision to ensure that electricity excise duty rates do not exceed those on natural gas, potentially reducing bills in some Member States.
